files.lesson.md: --- order: 2 unit: exponentials node: AC9M10A03 n2 uses: [AC9M8A04 n2] # where a line crosses the y-axis connection: cooling-tea title: Exponential graphs summary: "The graph of y = a(bˣ) crosses the y-axis at a, grows when b is more than 1, decays when b is between 0 and 1, and never reaches the line y = 0 when it decays." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Pour a cup of tea and leave it on the bench. Will it ever get colder than the room?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8391 url: http://127.0.0.1:8391/index.html readySelector: "#sl-a" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: graph.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$y = 80(0.5^x)$ starts at 80 and halves each step. It gets closer to $y = 0$ but never reaches it." } explainClip: query: { code: "@graph.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "b above 1 grows, b below 1 decays" say: "A base above one grows, and a base below one decays." clip: - caption: { text: "b = 2: the graph doubles each step and climbs.", say: "With b equal to two, the graph doubles each step and climbs." } - wait: 800 - click: Make b smaller - click: Make b smaller - click: Make b smaller - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "b = 0.5: it halves each step and falls towards 0.", say: "With b equal to one half, it halves each step and falls towards zero." } - caption: { text: "It never reaches the x-axis.", say: "It never reaches the x axis." } - wait: 1200 --- A cup of tea starts at 90 °C in a room at 20 °C. It cools quickly at first and then more slowly. The readings in this lesson are made up. In class you can take your own with a thermometer, every couple of minutes, and see how close they are. Will the tea ever get colder than the room? ## Predict: the next ten minutes ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to what the tea does in the second ten minutes shows who expects a steady fall (35 °C again, as a straight line would give) and who sees the cooling slow as the tea nears the room." check: type: predict q: "The tea starts at 90 °C. After 10 minutes it is 55 °C, a fall of 35 °C. What does it do in the next 10 minutes?" options: - "It falls by less than 35 °C" - "It falls by 35 °C again, to 20 °C" - "It falls by more than 35 °C" - "It stays at 55 °C" actual: "It falls by less than 35 °C. The hotter the tea is above the room, the faster it loses heat, so the cooling slows as the gap closes. With these made-up readings the gap to the room halves every 10 minutes: 35 °C, then 17.5 °C. So at 20 minutes the tea is 20 + 17.5 = 37.5 °C, a fall of 17.5 °C." ``` The two dots are the first two readings. Make a guess about the next one before you check. ## Run: the shape of y = a(bˣ) ```step stage: run insight: "Changing b turns the graph from growth to decay; changing a only moves where it starts. The decay graph keeps falling and the table never reaches 0." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#run", height: 660 } check: { type: board, text: "Set $b$ to 0.5, so the value halves every step. That's how the gap between the tea and the room behaves. Was your prediction right?", when: "b = 0.5" } ``` The board draws $y = a(b^x)$. $a$ is where it starts, and $b$ is what you multiply by each time $x$ goes up by 1. Change them and watch the graph and the table. ## Investigate: reading the graph ```step stage: investigate insight: "a is where the graph crosses the y-axis; b above 1 grows and b between 0 and 1 decays. A decay graph never reaches 0, however long it runs. Kim thinks repeated halving gets to 0." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Where does $y = 3(2^x)$ cross the $y$-axis? Give the value of $y$." answer: "3" feedback: - ["2", "2 is b, what you multiply by. The graph crosses the y-axis where x = 0: put 0 in."] - ["6", "6 is y when x = 1. The y-axis is where x = 0."] explain: "3. When x = 0, 2 to the power 0 is 1, so y = 3 × 1 = 3. That's a." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#kim" text: "Kim sketches $y = 4(0.5^x)$. Click the line where her reasoning goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: exp-reaches-zero explain: "Line 4: halving never gets to 0. 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125... there is always half left. The graph gets closer and closer to the x-axis but never touches it." - check: type: question q: "Which of these is a decay graph?" options: ["$y = 5(1.2^x)$", "$y = 5(0.8^x)$", "$y = 0.8(5^x)$"] answer: 1 feedback: ["1.2 is more than 1, so each step multiplies by more than 1. It grows.", null, "0.8 is a, where it starts. The base is 5, more than 1, so it grows."] explain: "y = 5(0.8^x) multiplies by 0.8 each step, so it gets smaller: decay. The base, the number with the x in its power, decides." ``` ### Where it starts Here is a decay graph worked out. ```worked y = 80(0.5^x) :: What does this graph do? x = 0:\; y = 80(0.5^0) = 80 :: Put 0 in. Any number to the power 0 is 1, so y is just a. It crosses the y-axis at 80. b = 0.5 < 1 :: The base is less than 1: each step multiplies by a half, so the graph decays. 80,\; 40,\; 20,\; 10,\; 5,\; 2.5 :: Keep halving for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. y > 0 \text{ always} :: Halving never gives 0, so y never touches the x-axis. y = 0 :: The graph gets closer and closer to y = 0 but never reaches it. A line it gets close to like this is called an asymptote. ``` Now try one on paper like the example: $y = 3(2^x)$. Where does it cross the $y$-axis, and does it grow or decay? Then type the $y$-axis value. ### Find the mistake Read Kim's working. Does repeated halving ever reach 0? ### Growth or decay Look at the number with the $x$ in its power. ## Modify: change a and b ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: match two points with a and b, make a decay graph, set b to 1, then step back to a negative x." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#vary", height: 620 } tasks: - starter: "graph.yml#through-5-10" hint: ["The graph crosses the y-axis at $P$. Which slider sets that?", "From $P$ to $Q$ the value doubles."] check: { type: board, text: "Make the graph pass through $P(0, 5)$ and $Q(1, 10)$.", when: "a = 5 and b = 2", explain: "a = 5 (where it starts) and b = 2 (10 is 2 times 5)." } - starter: "graph.yml#decay" hint: ["Where does it cross the y-axis?", "From 3 to 1.5, what do you multiply by?"] check: { type: board, text: "Make a decay graph through $P(0, 3)$ and $Q(1, 1.5)$.", when: "a = 3 and b = 0.5", explain: "a = 3, and b = 0.5 because 1.5 is half of 3. The graph falls." } - hint: "Set $b$ to 1 and look at the table." check: type: question q: "Edge case: set $b$ to 1. What does the graph look like?" options: ["A flat line at height $a$: it doesn't grow or decay", "A curve that grows slowly", "A curve that decays slowly"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so it can't grow.", "Multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so it can't decay."] explain: "Multiplying by 1 each step leaves the value where it is: a flat line at a." - hint: ["Going one step back divides by $b$.", "At $x = 0$, $y = 4$. At $x = -1$, divide by 2."] check: { type: answer, q: "Edge case: the graph $y = 4(2^x)$ goes backwards too. What is $y$ when $x = -1$?", answer: "2", feedback: [["8", "8 is y when x = 1. Going to x = −1 is one step back, so divide by 2."], ["-4", "A negative x doesn't make y negative. One step back from 4 divides by 2."]], explain: "One step back divides by 2: 4 ÷ 2 = 2. (2⁻¹ = 1/2, so 4 × 1/2 = 2.)" } ``` ### Two points, growth Each of the first two tasks gives you two points. Set $a$ and $b$ so the graph passes through both. ### Two points, decay ### A base of 1 ### Going backwards ## Practise: read the rule ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading the starting value, growth or decay, and the asymptote from the rule, with a review of the ratio from the last lesson." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Where does $y = 7(3^x)$ cross the $y$-axis? Give the value of $y$." answer: "7" feedback: - ["3", "3 is b. Put x = 0 in: 3 to the power 0 is 1."] - ["21", "21 is y when x = 1. The y-axis is where x = 0."] explain: "7. At x = 0, 3⁰ = 1 and y = 7 × 1 = 7." - check: type: question q: "Is $y = 100(0.9^x)$ growth or decay?" options: ["Decay: 0.9 is less than 1", "Growth: 100 is a big number", "Growth: 0.9 is positive"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "100 is a, where it starts. The base decides: 0.9.", "Positive isn't enough. Multiplying by 0.9 makes the value smaller each step."] explain: "The base 0.9 is between 0 and 1, so each step makes y smaller: decay." - check: type: answer q: "The graph of $y = 6(0.5^x)$ gets closer and closer to a horizontal line but never reaches it. What is $y$ on that line?" answer: "0" feedback: - ["6", "6 is where the graph starts (a). It falls from there."] - ["0.5", "0.5 is b. The line is where y ends up as the halving goes on and on."] explain: "0. Halving 6, 3, 1.5, 0.75... gets closer and closer to 0 and never reaches it. The line y = 0 is the asymptote." smaller: check: type: question q: "Keep halving: 6, 3, 1.5, 0.75, ... Will you ever get exactly 0?" options: ["Yes, after enough halvings", "No: there's always half left"] answer: 1 feedback: ["Try it: each half is still more than 0, however small.", null] explain: "Half of something that isn't 0 is never 0. The numbers get tiny but stay above 0." - check: type: answer q: "Review: the table goes $7, 14, 28, 56$. What do you multiply by each time?" answer: "2" feedback: - ["7", "7 is how far it goes up from 7 to 14. The ratio is 14 ÷ 7."] explain: "14 ÷ 7 = 2 and 28 ÷ 14 = 2. Each value is 2 times the one before." ``` ### Start ### Growth or decay ### Never reaches ### Review The ratio, from the last lesson. ## Make: back to the tea ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the cup: the gap to the room decays and never reaches 0, so the tea never goes below the room." try: { playground: board, starter: "graph.yml#tea", height: 600 } tasks: - hint: ["The gap starts at 70 °C and halves every 10 minutes.", "30 minutes is three halvings."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The tea is 90 °C in a 20 °C room. The gap between them starts at 70 °C and halves every 10 minutes (made-up readings). What is the tea's temperature after 30 minutes?" steps: - ["$70 \\div 2 = 35$ after 10 minutes", "the gap halves"] - ["$35 \\div 2 = 17.5$ after 20 minutes, then $17.5 \\div 2 = 8.75$ after 30", "halve twice more"] - ["$20 + 8.75 = 28.75$ °C", "the tea is the room plus the gap"] answer: "28.75" answerLabel: "Tea temperature (°C)" feedback: - ["8.75", "That's the gap. The tea is the room (20 °C) plus the gap."] - ["0", "The gap shrinks but doesn't reach 0, and the tea is still above the room."] criteria: - "I halved the gap three times." - "I added the room temperature back on." - "My tea is still warmer than the room." explain: "The gap: 70, 35, 17.5, 8.75. The tea is 20 + 8.75 = 28.75 °C." - check: type: question q: "Back to the question: will the tea ever get colder than the room?" options: ["No: the gap keeps halving but never reaches 0, so the tea stays above the room", "Yes, after about 70 minutes, when the gap has gone", "Yes, once the gap reaches 0 it keeps going down"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Halving 70 never lands on 0, so the gap never goes. Check the dashed line on the board.", "The gap never reaches 0, so there's no time when the tea has gone below the room."] explain: "The gap is a decay graph, and a decay graph never reaches 0. The tea gets closer to 20 °C, and the dashed line on the board is its asymptote." ``` ### Tea after 30 minutes Back to the cup. Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Colder than the room? Move $b$ on the board. A flask that keeps the heat in has a $b$ close to 0.9. Does the tea ever go below the dashed line? **Also used in** - **Hot food.** A pie out of the oven cools towards the kitchen's temperature the same way. - **Money.** A car that loses the same share of its value each year decays too, and its graph never quite reaches zero dollars. - **Next lessons.** Reading the rule $y = a(b^x)$ from a graph, and solving for when it reaches a number. ```teacher summary: Students draw y = a(bˣ) on a graph board, find that a is where it starts and b above or below 1 decides growth or decay, and see that a decay graph never reaches the asymptote y = 0, using a cooling cup of tea (AC9M10A03, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can read where an exponential graph starts from its rule. - I can say whether y = a(bˣ) grows or decays from b. - I can explain why a decay graph never reaches the x-axis. struggle: Believing repeated halving eventually reaches 0. Keep halving a number on paper or a calculator and look at how small it gets without ever being 0. before: > Do the Run and Modify boards yourself first. Students need the ratio from the last lesson (Same ratio each time) and where a line crosses the y-axis from Linear relations. The one idea: the base b decides growth (more than 1) or decay (between 0 and 1), and a decay graph gets closer and closer to y = 0 without reaching it. The tea comes back at the end: the gap between tea and room decays, so the tea settles above room temperature. All the tea readings are made up (tea at 90 °C, room at 20 °C, the gap halving every 10 minutes). Real readings follow a similar pattern, and your students' own will show how close. A class practical: hot (not boiling) water in a cup, a thermometer, a reading every 2 minutes for 20 minutes. Supervise the hot water. Plot the readings, then the gap to the room (tea minus room), and ask what shape the gap makes. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. The common wrong answer is 'it falls by 35 °C again, to 20 °C': students expect a steady fall." - "Run: ask students to read the table for b = 0.5 down the column: 16, 8, 4, 2... and say whether it ever hits 0." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the tea in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for the 20 °C added back on." - "Modify: before the base of 1, ask what multiplying by 1 does." stuck: - see: A student says a decay graph reaches 0 (Kim's mistake). ask: What is half of 0.001? And half of that? fix: "Halve a number several times on a calculator: it gets tiny but never 0. The graph gets as close to the axis as you like but never touches it." - see: A student reads b as where the graph crosses the y-axis. ask: What is y when x is 0? Put 0 in. fix: Anything to the power 0 is 1, so y = a. The y-axis crossing is a; b is what you multiply by. - see: A student says y = 0.8(5^x) is decay because of the 0.8. ask: Which number has the x in its power? fix: The base 5 decides. 0.8 is the starting value a. stretch: "Why can't b be negative? Try b = −1 on paper: −1, 1, −1, 1... Or: if the tea were at 5 °C in a 20 °C room, what would the gap do?" support: A table of the first six values of 80(0.5ˣ) with the x row and y row, and a halving arrow between neighbours. Draw the curve by hand from it. leads: > Next: reading the rule y = a(bˣ) from a graph (a from the start, b from the ratio of neighbours), then solving equations where x is in the power. Where it leads in class: modelling growth and decay (is it linear or exponential?), compound interest, and half-life. exit: q: "For y = 10(0.5ˣ): where does it cross the y-axis, does it grow or decay, and what line does it get close to but never reach?" a: At 10; decay; y = 0. explain: > In $y = a(b^x)$, $a$ is where the graph crosses the $y$-axis, because $b^0 = 1$. $b$ is what you multiply by each step. If $b > 1$ the graph **grows**. If $0 < b < 1$ it **decays**: the values get smaller but never reach 0. The line $y = 0$ is the **asymptote**: the graph gets as close as you like but never touches it. ```

# Boards for "Exponential graphs". y = a(b^x): a is the starting value (where the graph crosses the y-axis), b is
# what you multiply by each step. The "tea" board is the cooling cup: the room is 20 °C and the gap shrinks by b each
# 10-minute step (made-up readings).

# region: run
widget: graph
x: -3, 5
y: -2, 40
grid: 1, 10
slider a: 1, 5, 2
slider b: 0.5, 2, 2, 0.5
plot: y = a(b^x)
table: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: graph
x: -3, 5
y: -2, 40
grid: 1, 10
slider a: 1, 5, 2
slider b: 0.5, 2, 2, 0.5
plot: y = a(b^x)
table: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: graph
x: -1, 6
y: -10, 90
grid: 1, 20
plot: y = 80(0.5^x)
point A: 0, 80
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: graph
x: -3, 5
y: -2, 40
grid: 1, 10
slider a: 1, 8, 2
slider b: 0.5, 3, 2, 0.5
plot: y = a(b^x)
table: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2
# endregion

# region: through-5-10
widget: graph
x: -1, 4
y: -2, 24
grid: 1, 4
slider a: 1, 8, 2
slider b: 0.5, 3, 1, 0.5
plot: y = a(b^x)
point P: 0, 5
point Q: 1, 10
# endregion

# region: decay
widget: graph
x: -1, 4
y: -1, 10
grid: 1, 2
slider a: 1, 8, 2
slider b: 0.5, 3, 2, 0.5
plot: y = a(b^x)
point P: 0, 3
point Q: 1, 1.5
# endregion

# region: tea
widget: graph
x: 0, 6
y: 0, 100
grid: 1, 20
axes: Time (10-minute steps), Tea (°C)
slider b: 0.3, 0.9, 0.5, 0.1
plot: y = 20 + 70(b^x)
plot: y = 20, dashed
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
# endregion

# Kim's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: kim
Sketch y = 4 × 0.5^x.
When x = 0, y = 4, so the graph starts at 4.
0.5 is less than 1, so y gets smaller as x grows: 4, 2, 1, 0.5, ...
Keep halving and y reaches 0, so the graph crosses the x-axis.
# endregion
